title: Valve slowly expands SteamOS support on non-Valve hardware
gist: The SteamOS 3.8.25 Beta adds initial gamepad support for Intel-based and Android/Windows handhelds including MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, Ayaneo Pocket S2 and Konkr Fit, signalling Valve is still building its Linux OS into a cross-vendor handheld platform rather than a Steam Deck exclusive — though the Lenovo Legion Go S is still the only third-party device with full 'powered by SteamOS' branding.

themes.theme: SteamOS as a licensable third-party platform

insights.claim: Valve's SteamOS 3.8.25 Beta added initial gamepad support for MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, Ayaneo's Android-focused Pocket S2 and the Windows-based Konkr Fit, plus improved support for older MSI Claw and OneXPlayer devices.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Each added OEM device widens the installed base that could ship a Linux gaming OS instead of Windows, eroding Microsoft's default position in handheld PCs.
insights.locator: This weekend’s release of the SteamOS 3.8.25 Beta

insights.claim: Despite steady compatibility work across many OEM handhelds, Lenovo's Legion Go S remains the only non-Valve device carrying the full 'powered by SteamOS' branding that certifies complete compatibility.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The gap between 'controller works' and full certification is the real gating metric for SteamOS displacing Windows on OEM handhelds — watch the count of branded devices, not driver patch notes.
insights.quote: the Lenovo Legion Go S remains the only non-Valve device to sport the full “powered by SteamOS” branding
insights.locator: So far, the Lenovo Legion Go S remains

insights.claim: The author reads the incremental driver work as evidence Valve remains committed to making SteamOS run well across a broad third-party device fleet rather than treating it as Steam Deck-only firmware.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A generalized SteamOS is the strategic threat to Windows gaming; the pace is slow, which caps the near-term impact but keeps the option alive.
insights.quote: these kinds of updates suggest the company is still interested in getting its bespoke OS working well on plenty of other devices
insights.locator: So far, the Lenovo Legion Go S remains

themes.theme: Intel re-entering the handheld silicon conversation

insights.claim: SteamOS historically carried beta support only for AMD-powered handhelds, and Valve has only recently begun building compatibility for Intel-based handhelds such as the MSI Claw line.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: AMD's effective monopoly on Linux-friendly handheld gaming silicon is being chipped at; Intel gaining SteamOS parity would open a second-source market for handheld APUs.
insights.quote: While SteamOS has long included beta support for “other AMD powered handhelds,” Valve has only recently been working on offering compatibility with Intel-based handhelds
insights.locator: Those newly supported handhelds include MSI’s Claw 8 EX AI+

insights.claim: The newly supported MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is built around Intel's Arc G3 processor and launched this summer as an extremely expensive, extremely powerful handheld.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Intel's Arc graphics IP is landing in premium handhelds, giving Intel a halo showcase in a segment AMD has dominated.
insights.locator: Those newly supported handhelds include MSI’s Claw 8 EX AI+

insights.claim: June's SteamOS 3.8 release explicitly emphasized improved compatibility with recent Intel and AMD platforms and named controller improvements for GPD Win, Anbernic, OrangePi, Lenovo Legion Go, MSI Claw and OneXPlayer devices.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Two consecutive releases targeting third-party silicon and OEMs establish a trend line, not a one-off.
insights.locator: This weekend’s update follows June’s SteamOS 3.8 update

insights.claim: Valve updated the Linux driver for the new Steam Controller so it works with native controller applications even when the Steam client is not running, benefiting users running emulators or Linux-native non-Steam games in Desktop mode.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Valve making its hardware useful outside its own storefront signals it is optimizing for Linux ecosystem adoption over short-term store lock-in.
insights.locator: Elsewhere in the new SteamOS update
